extracted.intended_audience: readers or learners of Renaissance courtly behaviour (courtiers, students of literature and etiquette)
extracted.subtask_description: Dialogued advice (from The Third Book of The Courtier) on how a courtier should win, declare, maintain, and conceal a lady's favour — including recommended behaviours, precautions, and anti-patterns. Presented as normative social guidance in Renaissance courtly context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whoever would be loved must love and be lovable
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think, then, that whoever would be loved must love and be lovable; and that these two things suffice to win women's favour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emilia insists that genuine love requires both loving and being lovable; dispersing affections among many weakens the strength of love. Being lovable (merits, behaviour) is as essential as loving sincerely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin by pleasing and subordinating one's desires to the beloved
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who begins to love ought also to begin to please his beloved and bend himself wholly to her wishes, and govern his by hers; and make his own desires her slaves, and his very soul like unto an obedient handmaid...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True lovers should seek to transform their wishes to match the beloved's, treating their own desires as subordinate; this total attentiveness is presented as the law of love and the path to true loving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare love with modesty and caution; be sure not to offend before declaring
rubrics_metrics.description: “If he must speak or write, let him do it with such modesty and so warily that his first words shall try her mind... leave a way and certain loophole that may enable her to feign not to see that his discourse imports love... in order that he may retreat in case of difficulty...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a declaration, test the lady's disposition with ambiguous, modest phrasing that permits safe retreat. Ensure beforehand that declaration will not offend her; if unsure, prefer not to sue openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show love by manner rather than by words
rubrics_metrics.description: “The way that the Courtier ought to take to make his love known to the Lady... is by showing it to her in manner rather than in words;— for verily more of love's affection is sometimes revealed in a sigh, in reverence, in timidity, than in a thousand words.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonverbal signs (sighs, reverence, timidity) and comportment often communicate passion more suitably than explicit speech; favour subtlety of manner to preserve dignity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the eyes as faithful messengers but govern them with skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Long passage describing eyes as 'faithful messengers' that can disclose passion more clearly than tongue or letters; eyes can kindle love but must be governed cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make gentle, kind, well-timed glances to convey feeling; yet restrain gaze when necessary because uncontrolled looks may betray passion to unintended observers—observe time and place and abstain when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make demonstrations of love evident but modest
rubrics_metrics.description: “... besides loving and serving it is further necessary to make some other demonstration of his love so evident that the lady cannot hide her knowledge that she is loved; yet with such modesty withal that he may not seem to have small respect for her.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement service and affection with a modestly visible token or behaviour so the lady recognizes being loved without feeling affronted or disrespected; balance clarity with decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a lady's favour by pleasing her and avoiding offence
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think that those means which serve to win it serve also to maintain it; and all this consists in pleasing the lady of our love without ever offending her.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously please and serve the lady, and avoid behaviour (importunity, excessive lamenting, jealous outbursts) that may weary or offend her; discretion and moderation sustain favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Win over rivals by merit, not by deceit or slander
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would have him deprive his rival of the lady's favour by no other craft than by loving and serving her, and by being worthy, valiant, discreet and modest; in short, by deserving her better than his rival...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not employ slander or treachery; instead, outshine rivals through genuine service, worthiness, valour, discretion, and modesty. The text condemns malicious ruin of rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical rhetorical excesses and boastfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of anti-patterns: using 'Poliphilian words' that bewilder women, being immoderately boastful, or saying things like 'I have never found a woman to love me' which damage reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornate, overwrought rhetoric that makes women feel ignorant or bored; refrain from boastful or self-deprecating remarks that lessen esteem or invite derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep love affairs secret but not by over-secrecy; use trusted intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to keep love secret it is needful to avoid the causes that make it public... there is one chief cause, which is the wish to be too secret and not trust any person whatever... a friend... often contrives secrecy and provides for many things for which he himself cannot provide.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use faithful friends as intermediaries to reduce suspicious demonstrations; total secrecy through solitude forces excessive demonstrations that attract attention. Confiding judiciously helps preserve privacy and steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the dangers of public report and gossip; conceal ardour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Magnifico warns that loves conducted with report as minister put a man in danger of being pointed at; he advises feigning less fire, concealing desires, and often laughing when heart weeps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rumours circulate, one should appear less ardent to avoid spectacle; conceal jealousies and griefs, practice self-control, and avoid publicly publicising intimate affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ discreet signaling when conversing in public
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernardo's anecdote: lovers can hold a long and free love talk that others cannot understand because speakers whisper only the words that signify and speak the rest aloud so it can be construed differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speaking where others listen, use careful, partial whispering and ambiguous statements to communicate privately without exposing content to onlookers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'sue in love' unless certain of not being repulsed
rubrics_metrics.description: “All women like to be sued in love, even though they mean to refuse... You are very wrong; nor should I advise the Courtier ever to employ this method, unless he be certain of not being repulsed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue open courtship (suing) only when reasonably confident of acceptance; reckless approaches risk public humiliation and loss of esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempts to destroy a rival by malicious exposure; favor prudent dissimulation only if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of two methods: pretending friendship until opportunity to overwhelm rival with evil (true or false) versus the Magnifico's preference for winning by worth and service; the proverb about lifting or drowning an enemy illustrates the choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text exposes malicious tactics of ruin and advocates restraint: prefer to excel by merit; if dissimulation is used, be wary of moral cost and risk to one's own honour.
